failure_summary.description: Three runs chose an inflated option whose extra clause is an unproved rider (data-only estimate, structure of the leftover set, cross-index compatibility). One run chose the bare 'is rational' corollary over the competing explicit-formula options.

Missed an isolated swap (λ placement) even though every other option agreed. Chose an option that unpacks a stem-defined term plus a side condition over the option using the term verbatim. Preferred a constant copied from the stem (2ℓ) over the derived one (ℓ).
Did not use the threshold hypothesis (γ>1) to fix the exponent, although a priority rule already covers it.

patch.reasoning: Most of these failures are already covered by existing rules (odd-one-out swap, defined-term verbatim, zero-data test, exponent threshold, bare-corollary warning). The target still did not apply them, so this is a salience problem and not a missing-rule problem. The patch puts one short, visibly executable decision order at the top. It diffs every option against the plain one, kills options on structure first, then separates UPGRADES (formula or value of the named quantity, stronger mode) from RIDERS (estimates, leftover-set structure, cross-index compatibility, extremality, wider quantification). The riders are listed by option structure, with no topic-specific content. It adds a truncation check for the opposite error: a bare option implied by several others loses unless every stronger option fails a test. It adds a short warning against copying constants literally from the stem. One topic-specific bullet is deleted to keep the document length roughly flat.

edits.content:
## Decision checklist (write it out visibly; it overrides the gist of any option)
1. Plain option P = the natural theorem in the stem's own objects and parameters. Write every other option as 'P + delta' or 'P with X swapped'.
2. Kill by structure BEFORE any strength reasoning: (a) isolated swap: if options differ in where a coefficient, index or term sits, count options per placement and the lone placement is dead, even if it is listed first; (b) a deleted, relaxed or changed stem hypothesis, range or parameter; (c) in 'equivalent to / iff' stems, an option that unpacks a stem-defined term and adds a side condition (narrower class) is only implied by the target, and the option using the defined term verbatim wins; (d) 'only / need not / least energy / unique' tails.
3. Classify each surviving delta. UPGRADE (may keep): an explicit formula or value for the very quantity the stem names; a stronger mode of the same conclusion; a 'moreover, if H' with H stated inside the option. RIDER (drop unless you can derive it in a few lines): a quantitative estimate or constant; a description of the leftover / exceptional / bad set; compatibility across several indices or objects (all m, products of bases) when the stem fixes one; minimality, extremality or uniqueness; any quantification wider than the one the stem fixes.
4. Test each delta you keep on one degenerate case (zero data, n=1, smallest example, parameter to 0). A delta that fails, or that you cannot test, is a rider.
5. Constant lure: a number or symbol copied literally from the stem (e.g. '2ℓ' from '2ℓ twists') is not evidence. Check whether the stem's factor is already absorbed by the invariant (half-twists vs full twists, factor 2) and recompute the induced change before choosing between ℓ and 2ℓ.

edits.target: 6. Do not default to the bare, minimal, or hedged option because it feels safe.
edits.content: 6. Do not default to the bare, minimal, or hedged option because it feels safe. Truncation check: if a bare option (membership, 'is rational', first clause only) is implied by two or more other options, it is their common weakening. Under 'exact / strongest / which holds for every', it is correct only if every stronger option contains a clause that actually FAILS a concrete test (e.g. a data-only estimate fails the zero-data test). Otherwise choose among the stronger options by a degenerate-case computation, not by default.

edits.target: - For numerical-bound questions (kissing numbers, packing densities, etc.), 'strongest that holds' means the best bound actually established. Larger numbers are often fabricated over-claims. Anchor on the best known bound you can recall, and be sceptical of any lower bound above the known record.
